cards.f: The whole lecture follows one patient through three stages?
cards.b: (1) uncomplicated colic → hydration · analgesia · medical expulsive therapy; (2) obstructed + infected kidney → cultures → broad-spectrum antibiotics → urgent urine diversion (DJ stent); (3) infection cleared (negative culture) → definitive stone treatment chosen by site and size.
a 24-year-old male presented with left flank pain for 2 days. Next?
onset (sudden?), duration, severity (often 10/10), radiation loin → groin, aggravating/relieving factors, relation to movement
haematuria, dysuria, frequency, urgency — their absence does not exclude a stone. Eliminate the differentials: GI symptoms, fever (infection changes everything), chest, gynae and testicular symptoms
general examination · abdominal examination · costovertebral angle tenderness.
vital signs — fever, tachycardia, hypotension point to sepsis
peritonism/guarding, masses, a pulsatile mass (aneurysm), palpable bladder. CVA tenderness localises the problem to the kidney.

older patient with a "first ever" renal colic → think leaking AAA (feel for a pulsatile mass, check BP) · woman of reproductive age → pregnancy test (ectopic), consider ovarian torsion · young male with groin pain → always examine the testes (torsion) · referred upper-abdominal pain with risk factors → ECG for MI; peritonism → perforated ulcer. Radicular pain varies with movement.

drug levels are low in an obstructed system that isn't draining. Definitive treatment now → sepsis — manipulating a stone in an infected obstructed system pushes bacteria into the blood. Rule: drain first, treat the stone later — after a negative urine culture.
